title: Why Is Nashville Called Music City? Legend Credits a Queen
description:
Taylor Swift's return to the CMA Awards in Nashville was in the news this week. So why is Nashville called Music City? Legend gives the credit to Queen Victoria and to the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a group of students who sang to save their school.
🚶 Visiting San Diego? Explore its history on a guided tour with Fable: https://fablehospitality.com

Every frame is drawn with code. No stock footage, no AI video.

0:00 Why "Music City"?
0:06 The legend: a queen and a few students
0:09 1871: Fisk University is nearly broke
0:15 October 6, 1871: George White takes nine students on the road
0:20 Born into slavery
0:23 The Jubilee Singers and their spirituals
0:27 1873: singing for Queen Victoria
0:31 "A city of music"? The story goes...
0:35 The portrait that still hangs at Fisk
0:41 About $150,000 raised
0:44 1876: Jubilee Hall
0:49 WSM, home of the Grand Ole Opry
0:56 "Music City USA"
0:59 Jubilee Day

Note: Fisk University (founded 1866 for freed people) was close to closing in 1871. On October 6, 1871, treasurer and music teacher George L. White left Nashville with nine student singers; several had been born into slavery. Their spirituals made them famous: they sang for Queen Victoria in 1873, and over their tours (1871-1878) they raised about $150,000, which built Jubilee Hall, Fisk's first permanent building (dedicated January 1, 1876). A large portrait of the singers, given by the queen, hangs at Fisk. The popular story that Victoria said they must come from a "city of music" is a legend with no firm record; most accounts credit the nickname "Music City, U.S.A." to WSM radio announcer David Cobb, on air around 1950 (some sources say 1960). Fisk marks October 6 as Jubilee Day.

Images (public domain): Queen Victoria, engraving after a photograph by W. & D. Downey, from A. E. Knight, Victoria: Her Life and Reign (1896); George L. White and the group photograph of the Jubilee Singers, from J. B. T. Marsh, The Story of the Jubilee Singers (1880); Thomas Rutling, Maggie Porter and Benjamin M. Holmes, engravings from photographs by Black, from G. D. Pike, The Jubilee Singers and Their Campaign for Twenty Thousand Dollars (1873); "Jubilee Hall, Fisk University", engraving from Marsh (1880); cover of Jubilee Songs, as Sung by the Jubilee Singers of Fisk University (1872, Emory University via Internet Archive). Documents drawn in code.
Maps drawn in code from Natural Earth (world-atlas) and US Census (us-atlas) outlines.
Narration voice is synthetic.
